courseTitle: The ABA problem and tagged pointers
lessonTitle: Tagged pointers: a version counter beside the pointer
md: Tagged pointer = pointer plus a counter compared and swapped as one unit, bumped on every successful CAS. It turns "same value" into "same value and same version".

courseTitle: Ablation studies: what each pipeline stage really adds
lessonTitle: Per-query deltas, paired tests and confidence intervals
md: Queries are not the only noise source. If a stage is trained, its score also varies with the random seed. Use the same seeds and checkpoints for every stage you are not ablating, and when the ablated stage itself is retrained, run several seeds and report the spread, or a seed-to-seed swing can masquerade as a component effect.

courseTitle: Broken access control and authorization design
lessonTitle: Sequential vs random ids, and why random ids are not authorization
md: Parler's public posts were meant to be readable one at a time. Sequential ids plus no rate limit turned "anyone can read a post" into "anyone can copy the entire site, with GPS locations". Authorization decides who may read an object; rate limits and unpredictable ids decide how cheaply someone can read all of them. You need both.

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: What Active Directory is: one directory for thousands of machines
md: A domain is not a wall. Domains in one forest trust each other automatically, and the Enterprise Admins group of the forest root is an administrator in every domain (next lesson). Plan protection for the whole forest, not one domain at a time.

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: AS-REP roasting and password spraying against AD
md: Turning off pre-authentication hands out crackable material to anyone; 4768 with pre-auth type 0 finds it. Spraying hides under per-account lockout; count distinct accounts per source in 4771 and 4776, not failures per account.

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: Tiered administration, Protected Users and LAPS
md: Tiering fails quietly through agents. A backup, monitoring or patching tool that runs as SYSTEM on DCs, managed from a Tier 1 console, makes that console Tier 0. List everything installed on DCs and everyone who controls it.

courseTitle: Advanced memory exploitation concepts: ROP, heap and kernel
lessonTitle: Format string bugs as read and write primitives
md: A format string bug is a primitive factory: the read directives leak, and %n writes. The cure is structural and cheap: constant format strings, enforced by -Werror=format-security and static analysis.

courseTitle: Agent benchmarks: SWE-bench, tau-bench and reading the scores
lessonTitle: Reading a leaderboard: harness, noise, cost and contamination
md: Checklist for any agent leaderboard number: which subset and version; which harness, tools, step and cost budget; one attempt or best of many (pass@k vs pass^1 vs pass^k); how many tasks and trials, with an interval; and whether the tasks predate the model's training cutoff.

courseTitle: Agent long-term memory: what to store, update, retrieve and forget
lessonTitle: Why an agent cannot just replay its whole history
md: A memory system is defined by four decisions: what to write, how to reconcile it with what is already stored, what to retrieve for a given step, and what to forget. Retrieval alone is RAG; the write and forget decisions are what make it memory.

courseTitle: Agent verification: checking an agent's work before you trust it
lessonTitle: Best-of-N with an imperfect verifier: the accuracy ceiling
md: FPR sets the ceiling, TPR sets the speed. With enough samples, best-of-N accuracy converges to the verifier's precision $pt / (pt + (1-p)f)$. Raising TPR only means you need fewer samples to get there.

courseTitle: AI and LLM security: prompt injection, agents and model risks
lessonTitle: Prompt injection: when data becomes instructions
md: Treat every token the model reads as a possible instruction from whoever wrote it. You cannot reliably make the model ignore it, so limit what obeying it can achieve.

courseTitle: AI and LLM security: prompt injection, agents and model risks
lessonTitle: System prompt leakage and sensitive information disclosure
md: Assume the system prompt will be read by users and attackers. Put nothing in it that would hurt if published, and enforce every rule that matters in code.

courseTitle: AI for materials discovery: stability, GNoME and MatterGen
lessonTitle: A crystal as data: lattice, fractional coordinates, periodicity
md: A crystal is a set of atom types, fractional coordinates in [0, 1), and a 3x3 lattice. Cartesian position is $f$ times $L$, coordinates wrap mod 1, and every distance must use the minimum image.

courseTitle: Watermarking AI outputs
lessonTitle: Detection is a z-test on the green count
md: A tiny false positive rate is not zero at scale. $z > 4$ means a one-sided p of $3.2 \times 10^{-5}$: scan a million human documents and expect about 32 false flags. Hugging Face's `WatermarkDetector` defaults to $z > 3$, where the rate is $1.3 \times 10^{-3}$. Pick the threshold for the cost of a false accusation.

courseTitle: Anomaly and outlier detection
lessonTitle: Why the mean and standard deviation hide outliers
md: Masking is the main failure of mean-based scores: several outliers inflate the standard deviation and hide one another. The NIST handbook also warns that applying a single-outlier test repeatedly does not fix this, because the first test may already report nothing.

courseTitle: Anomaly and outlier detection
lessonTitle: Evaluating detectors when 1 percent of points are anomalies
md: Do not report accuracy for anomaly detection: labeling everything normal scores 99 percent accuracy here. Be wary of ROC-AUC alone too. Report AP or a PR curve, plus precision@k at the review budget you actually have.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: OAuth 2.0: delegated access without sharing a password
md: Misconception: "Sign in with X" means OAuth logged you in. Plain OAuth only says some client got a token. Building login on raw access tokens has caused real impersonation bugs; OpenID Connect adds the missing pieces.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: Validating a JWT correctly: algorithm, signature, iss, aud, exp, nbf
md: Misconception: "we validate the token at the API gateway, so services can just decode it." Then any path around the gateway, and any token for another audience the gateway also accepts, reaches services that trust it blindly. Each service should at least check the audience meant for it.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: What an application security programme is, and who owns what
md: "Security owns security" is the most common misconception. A central team that tries to fix everything becomes a bottleneck and then gets bypassed. The working model: developers own fixes, the security team owns the system that makes fixes happen.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: Testing the running app: DAST, IAST, SCA recall and fuzzing in CI
md: No method sees everything. SAST and SCA see code and dependencies early; DAST sees the deployed surface; IAST sees runtime paths the tests exercise; fuzzing sees parsers under abuse. Pick by what your application does: an API with a heavy parser needs fuzzing more than a static brochure site does.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: Metrics that matter: time to remediate, open age and coverage
md: Measure what is still open and what you cannot see. Mean time to remediate, open age, SLA compliance and coverage together describe a programme; any one alone can be gamed by accident.

courseTitle: Asymmetric embeddings: query vs document input types
lessonTitle: Why a question is not a short version of its answer
md: Misconception: *a text's embedding is a fixed property of the text.* In a role-aware model the same string gets one vector as a query and a different vector as a document, by design. Which vector you get depends on how you called the model.

courseTitle: Calling LLM APIs at scale: concurrency, rate limits, retries, caching
lessonTitle: Rate limits as token buckets: RPM, token limits and headers
md: Do not cache or replay a 429 as if it were an answer. RFC 6585 says responses with status 429 "MUST NOT be stored by a cache". Also note that a 429 is not always temporary: Anthropic returns 429 without a `retry-after` header when an organization reaches its monthly spend cap, and retrying keeps failing until access resumes.

courseTitle: Atomics and compare-and-swap (CAS)
lessonTitle: Why counter++ from two threads loses updates
md: `volatile` does not fix this. In C and C++ it stops the compiler from removing or reordering accesses within one thread, which suits signal handlers and memory-mapped I/O, but cppreference states it is not suitable for communication between threads. A volatile `counter++` is still a separate read and write.

courseTitle: Audio embeddings and classification
lessonTitle: Sigmoid outputs and pooling patch scores into a clip score
md: Mean pooling suits sounds that last (rain, engine hum, music) and resists one-patch glitches. Max pooling catches short events (a bark, a door slam, a gunshot) but turns any single false patch into a clip-level false alarm. PANNs combines both inside the network: its global pooling sums the time-averaged and the time-maximized feature vectors.

courseTitle: Authentication and identity attacks
lessonTitle: Slow on purpose: bcrypt, scrypt, Argon2id and cost parameters
md: Store passwords with Argon2id (or scrypt, or bcrypt for legacy), a unique salt per user, and a cost tuned as high as your login traffic allows. Record the parameters with each hash, and raise them over time.

courseTitle: Authentication and identity attacks
lessonTitle: Passkeys and WebAuthn: why phishing stops working
md: Passkeys resist phishing because the browser binds every signature to the real site's origin and the credential to the site's domain. The user's judgment is not part of the security argument.

courseTitle: Amazon Bedrock and the AWS generative AI stack
lessonTitle: One API in front of many models: the Converse call
md: Converse unifies the **shape** of requests and responses, not the **behavior** of models. Models still differ in quality, context length, supported content types and tool support, which the docs list per model. A one-line modelId swap is easy; validating that the new model is good enough is still your job.

courseTitle: 1.58-bit LLMs: ternary weights, BitLinear and bitnet.cpp
lessonTitle: BitLinear: a matrix multiply made of additions
md: "Matmul becomes additions" applies to the weight matrices. Attention scores (queries Q times keys K, then the attention weights times values V) multiply activations by activations, so they are not ternary. And the speedup only appears with a kernel that actually exploits ternary weights, which lesson 5 covers.

courseTitle: Branch prediction and branchless code
lessonTitle: Branchless code: cmov, masks and lookup tables
md: `cmov` with a memory operand always reads memory, even when the condition is false (the Intel pseudocode does `temp := SRC` first and lists page faults as possible). So a compiler cannot turn `p ? *p : 0` into a cmov from `*p`: it would fault on a null pointer. C's `?:` only evaluates the chosen side; branchless code evaluates both.

courseTitle: B-trees vs LSM-trees and compaction
lessonTitle: Leveled vs tiered compaction: counting write, read and space cost
md: Leveled: low space and read amplification, high write amplification. Tiered: low write amplification, more runs to read and up to about 2x temporary space during a full merge. The size ratio T slides each policy along its curve.

courseTitle: Tokenizer-free and byte-level models
lessonTitle: Why drop the tokenizer, and why raw bytes are expensive
md: Common misconception: byte models are slow because attention is quadratic. Efficient attention (methods and kernels such as FlashAttention that make attention cheaper or faster) helps small models, but the BLT authors point out that at scale the cost is dominated by the large feed-forward layers that run on **every** position. Fewer positions through the big network is what matters.

courseTitle: C and Rust: from malloc and free to ownership and unsafe
lessonTitle: Why C memory bugs compile cleanly and ship
md: C's type system cannot express *who owns this block* or *how long this pointer is valid*. Rust's ownership and borrow rules are exactly that missing information, checked at compile time.

courseTitle: Cache hierarchy (L1/L2/L3) and cache lines
lessonTitle: Cache lines: the cache moves 64 bytes, never just one
md: A common misconception is that memory cost is proportional to the bytes your code reads. It is proportional to the **lines it touches**. Reading 8 bytes from each of 1,000 scattered lines moves 64,000 bytes through the hierarchy.

courseTitle: Circuit tracing and attribution graphs
lessonTitle: The local replacement model makes every edge linear
md: Matching the real model's outputs exactly on prompt $p$ does not mean the local replacement model uses the same mechanism. The paper compares it to a Taylor approximation: it agrees at the point and drifts as you move away, which is why interventions are needed later.

courseTitle: Click models and unbiased learning to rank
lessonTitle: Small propensities, high variance, and clipping
md: Clipping changes what the estimator measures. A clipped rank is systematically undervalued, which pushes documents shown low back down, the same direction as the original position bias. Tune $\tau$ on held-out data and report it.

courseTitle: XSS, CSRF and client-side attacks
lessonTitle: Second lines of defence: strict CSP and Trusted Types
md: Trusted Types changes the review question from "is any of our thousands of DOM writes unsafe?" to "are our two or three policies correct?". The browser enforces that nothing else reaches a sink.

courseTitle: CLIP and image embeddings: learning vision from captions
lessonTitle: Image search with CLIP, the modality gap, and where it fails
md: Do not compare scores across modalities with one threshold. Image-image cosines and text-image cosines come from different regions of the space, so a cutoff tuned for text queries will not transfer to image queries, and a mixed index of image and text vectors will tend to rank same-modality items together.

courseTitle: Cloud security and IAM
lessonTitle: Storage exposure: public buckets, Block Public Access and SAS tokens
md: Turn on the provider's public-access guardrail at the highest level you can (organization or account), and treat any exception as a reviewed, documented decision. Then scan for anything public anyway: IAM Access Analyzer in AWS reports buckets shared publicly or with other accounts.

courseTitle: Clustering: k-means, DBSCAN and finding failure patterns
lessonTitle: Choosing k: elbow, silhouette and their limits
md: Three criteria, three answers on the same ten points: the elbow is ambiguous, VRC says k = 5, silhouette says k = 3. That disagreement is the lesson. Schubert's advice is to use a baseline-aware criterion (VRC, BIC or the gap statistic) rather than an elbow, and to spend your effort on preprocessing, "because garbage in, garbage out".

courseTitle: Columnar storage and vectorized execution
lessonTitle: SIMD, compiled queries and where columnar engines hit limits
md: Columnar storage cuts bytes moved; vectorized execution cuts instructions per byte. SIMD multiplies the second only when data is dense and in cache.

courseTitle: Compilers and optimization levels (-O2, LTO, inlining)
lessonTitle: PGO, -march=native and -ffast-math: speed with strings attached
md: -ffast-math assumes no NaNs or infinities (-ffinite-math-only), so code that relies on IEEE behavior of NaNs and infinities can give incorrect results. Clang has deprecated -Ofast because an optimization flag changing the observable behavior of correct code surprises people. Enable fast-math per file or per function when you have verified the numerics, not globally.

courseTitle: Concurrency testing with loom and ThreadSanitizer
lessonTitle: Why a concurrent test can pass a million times and still be wrong
md: An atomic load followed by an atomic store is **not** an atomic read-modify-write. The fix here is `num.fetch_add(1, AcqRel)`, which makes L and S one indivisible step. Atomics remove data races; they do not remove race conditions in your logic.

courseTitle: Consistency models and one-step diffusion
lessonTitle: Why one big ODE step from noise collapses to the mean
md: A diffusion model knows the *local* direction at each point. One-step generation needs the *global* answer: where does the whole trajectory end? A consistency model learns that endpoint directly.

courseTitle: Consistent hashing and hot-key mitigation
lessonTitle: Why hash mod N reshuffles almost every key
md: The goal of consistent hashing: when the set of servers changes, move only the keys that must move, which is about $K/N$ keys for $K$ keys and $N$ servers, and never shuffle keys between servers that did not change.

courseTitle: Constraint satisfaction: hard filters, then soft scoring
lessonTitle: Decay functions turn distance and recency into smooth scores
md: A missing field scores **1**, the best possible decay value, in both Elasticsearch and OpenSearch. Profiles with no location beat everyone who lives a few kilometers away. Decide explicitly: require the field with an `exists` filter (it keeps only documents that have a value in that field), index a default value, or accept the behavior on purpose.

courseTitle: Constraint satisfaction solvers: backtracking, AC-3, CDCL and CP-SAT
lessonTitle: CP-SAT in practice: lazy clauses, models and statuses
md: A solver turns a declarative model into search plus propagation plus learning. Your job is the model: tight domains, global constraints instead of many small ones, integer scaling, and a time limit with a status check.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: A hardened pod spec, line by line
md: Misconception: "runAsNonRoot is enough". It stops UID 0, but a non-root process with `allowPrivilegeEscalation` left at its default of true can still become root through a setuid binary in the image. Set both, and drop capabilities.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Pod Security Admission and policy engines
md: Label every namespace with a Pod Security level: Restricted for applications, Baseline at minimum, Privileged only for reviewed system namespaces. Add a policy engine for rules PSA cannot express, and treat its webhook as critical infrastructure.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Runtime detection with Falco and the Kubernetes audit log
md: Use both views: the audit log for who changed what through the API, and a syscall-level sensor such as Falco for what processes actually do. Each covers the other's blind spot.

courseTitle: Conversational query refinement: tracking search state across turns
lessonTitle: A five-turn session: diffs, state and generated queries
md: Strict mode guarantees the diff is **schema-valid**, not that it is **right**. A perfectly typed `{"remove": []}` for *drop the salary limit* is still a wrong state. Schema enforcement removes parsing failures; only evaluation (lesson 6) catches meaning failures.

courseTitle: Chain-of-thought faithfulness and monitorability
lessonTitle: Plausible is not faithful: the biasing-feature test
md: Faithfulness is a causal claim about what drove the answer. You test it by intervening, not by reading. A biasing feature that flips answers without ever being mentioned proves the CoT omitted a real cause.

courseTitle: CPU and GPU co-scheduling: streams, pinned memory and overlap
lessonTitle: A worked pipeline: four chunks, and the copy-bound crossover
md: Overlap hides the smaller stages behind the largest one; it never removes the largest one. Your speedup ceiling is $(\sum_s t_s) / (\max_s t_s)$, reached as $n$ grows, and in the steady state the pipeline runs at the rate of its slowest stage. Before adding streams, work out which stage that is. If it is already the kernel, overlap buys you the copies and nothing more.

courseTitle: Cross-encoder rerankers: scoring query and document together
lessonTitle: Serving it: latency for 100 candidates and distillation
md: Reranker latency is about k divided by throughput. You control it with three knobs: how many candidates you rerank, how large the model is, and how many pairs you can run in parallel. Each trades against accuracy or cost.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: MACs and HMAC: integrity with a shared key
md: Never build a MAC from hash(key + message), and never compare secrets with ==. Use HMAC (or an AEAD, which includes a MAC) and hmac.compare_digest.

courseTitle: CUTLASS and CuTe: tiling GEMMs across the GPU memory hierarchy
lessonTitle: CuTe layouts: shape and stride as an index function
md: A CuTe layout is not limited to row- or column-major, and the index it returns is in elements of whatever it is applied to, not bytes. The same function can index global memory, shared memory, registers, or even map thread ids to coordinates.

courseTitle: CXL and memory disaggregation: far memory you can load and store
lessonTitle: Why servers strand DRAM and why DDR alone cannot fix it
md: Pooling does not make stranding vanish. In the toy pooled design, host D still has 64 GB of local DRAM it cannot sell. Pooling helps because the *peaks* of different hosts rarely line up, so a shared buffer can be smaller than the sum of per-host slack.

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: Curation inside a domain: quality filters from phi-1 to FineWeb-Edu
md: Think in two levels. **Within** a domain, filter documents (deduplicate, drop low-quality pages with a classifier). **Across** domains, choose weights with a method like DoReMi or a fitted mixing model. Then rerun the mixing step, because filtering changes each domain's size and difficulty.

courseTitle: Deterministic inference: bitwise equivalence and reproducibility
lessonTitle: Two orderings, two answers: float addition is not associative
md: Floating-point addition is commutative but not associative. Reordering a sum is not a refactor, it is a different computation. Every other idea in this course follows from that sentence.

courseTitle: Diffusion language models: generating text by unmasking
lessonTitle: Why generate text in any order other than left to right?
md: A diffusion language model keeps the Transformer and the maximum-likelihood goal of a GPT. It changes two things: attention is bidirectional, and generation fills in many masked positions per step in any order instead of one token at the end.

courseTitle: Disaggregated prefill and decode
lessonTitle: Goodput: requests per GPU that meet both SLOs
md: Goodput is not throughput. A colocated GPU at 4 req/s still produces plenty of tokens per second, but in the toy run only 29% of requests meet both SLOs. If you only tracked throughput, that overloaded point would look like the best one.

courseTitle: DiskANN and CAGRA: billion-scale ANN on SSDs and GPUs
lessonTitle: DiskANN search: beam width, SSD reads and re-ranking
md: Beam width W trades round trips for wasted reads; search list L trades reads for recall. Tune L for the recall target first, then pick the smallest W that meets the latency target, watching total reads against the SSD's IOPS budget.

courseTitle: DPO and its variants: preference tuning without RL
lessonTitle: ORPO and SimPO: dropping the reference model
md: "Reference-free" also means there is no explicit KL anchor to the starting model. ORPO's SFT term and SimPO's length normalization and margin are what keep these losses from degenerating, and the SimPO authors stress that hyperparameter tuning matters for every **offline** method (one that trains on a fixed dataset instead of sampling new answers from the policy), DPO included.

courseTitle: Online data migration (dual-write and backfill)
lessonTitle: Proving the new read path before trusting it
md: Switch reads only when sustained, high-volume comparison shows zero unexplained mismatches, and keep dual writes running so the switch can be undone by a flag.

courseTitle: eBPF tracing with bpftrace: probes, verifier, maps
lessonTitle: Overhead, pitfalls and using bpftrace in production
md: Estimate cost as event rate x cost per event. Keep the rate low (stable, specific probes; filters; sampling) and keep the work in the kernel (maps, not printf). That is what makes bpftrace usable on a live production system.

courseTitle: Efficient reasoning: overthinking and length control
lessonTitle: Length penalties inside RL: Kimi k1.5 and DAPO
md: A length term changes which correct answers GRPO reinforces most. Without it, all correct answers in a group are equal; with it, the shortest correct one gets the largest advantage.

courseTitle: Energy disaggregation (NILM): from Hart's edges to seq2point
lessonTitle: Running edge detection and ON/OFF matching on the toy house
md: Event-based NILM reads each step as one appliance switching. When two appliances switch inside one sample, the switch continuity assumption breaks: the net step looks like a third, unrelated appliance, and the ON/OFF bookkeeping fails for both. Higher sample rates make such coincidences rarer but never impossible.

courseTitle: Entity normalization: job titles, schools and companies
lessonTitle: Scoring pairs with Fellegi-Sunter match weights
md: Each field adds $\log_2(m/u)$. Agreement on a rare value (a domain) is worth far more than agreement on a common one (a city), and a missing field adds nothing instead of counting as a disagreement.

courseTitle: epoll and event loops: serving many sockets from one thread
lessonTitle: Level-triggered versus edge-triggered, and reading until EAGAIN
md: Level-triggered asks "is it ready now?" on every wait. Edge-triggered says "it just became ready" once. With ET you own the state: read or write until `EAGAIN`, or remember that the connection is still ready.

courseTitle: Avoiding overfitting to a public query set
lessonTitle: Testing many variants: Bonferroni and Holm corrections
md: Count every comparison you make on a query set, including metrics, variants and earlier papers' tests, and correct for the family. Holm is never worse than Bonferroni. Better still, decide the one comparison you will test before you look.

courseTitle: Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI
lessonTitle: RELRO, the GOT and FORTIFY_SOURCE
md: RELRO protects a table of pointers by making it read-only after start-up; FORTIFY stops some overflows before they write. Both are cheap, both are build flags, and both should be on: `-Wl,-z,relro,-z,now` and `-D_FORTIFY_SOURCE=3` at `-O2`.

courseTitle: False sharing and cache-line padding
lessonTitle: Fixing it: pad, align, or stop sharing writes
md: A fix needs both size and alignment: each hot item must start on a line boundary and be at least a line long. And pad only data that different threads write often; group everything else tightly.

courseTitle: Federated learning: training without moving the data
lessonTitle: What the server sees: secure aggregation, DP, and Flower
md: The one thing to remember: federated learning is an optimization algorithm shaped by a systems constraint. Every piece (averaging instead of gradient sharing, a quorum instead of a barrier, masks instead of raw updates, noise instead of trust) exists because rounds are expensive, clients are unreliable, and the server is not allowed to look.

courseTitle: Fine-grained MoE, shared experts, aux-loss-free load balancing
lessonTitle: Aux-loss-free balancing: steer the router with a bias
md: The bias changes **which** experts a token uses, never **how much** a chosen expert contributes, and it receives no gradient. That is how Loss-Free Balancing controls load without fighting the language-modeling objective.

courseTitle: FlashInfer: an attention engine for LLM serving
lessonTitle: Tile sizes, GQA head fusion and JIT attention variants
md: FlashInfer = one block-sparse view of every KV layout, attention states merged exactly so work can be split and composed freely, a per-step plan that balances skewed lengths while staying CUDA-graph friendly, and a JIT template so new variants get fused kernels instead of new libraries.

courseTitle: Formal verification of systems code (TLA+, Verus)
lessonTitle: Verus: proving Rust functions with requires, ensures and invariants
md: Writing the invariant as `idx < n` looks natural but is wrong twice. Verus reports "invariant not satisfied before loop" (n can be 0) and "invariant not satisfied at end of loop body" (the last iteration makes idx == n).

courseTitle: FP8 and FP4 training: E4M3, scaling, MXFP4 and NVFP4
lessonTitle: NVFP4: 16-value blocks, E4M3 scales and a tensor scale
md: In NVFP4 the amax of every 16-value block is encoded at close to FP8 precision (the block scale is E4M3), which is at least 1/16 = 6.25% of all values. MXFP4 stores every value, the amax included, at FP4 precision behind a power-of-two scale.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: A real hunt with libFuzzer: harness, run log and the crash
md: On macOS, Apple's Xcode clang ships without libFuzzer (the Atheris documentation says the same), and Homebrew's clang needs the SDK path (`-isysroot $(xcrun --show-sdk-path)`) to find system headers. On Linux, distribution clang packages include it.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: Protocol and stateful fuzzing, and the Broadcom Wi-Fi case
md: The Broadcom case was found by reverse engineering and code review, not fuzzing, and its lesson for fuzzers is about reach: the dangerous code ran only for specific frame types in specific connection states. A stateless fuzzer of single frames would rarely get there.

courseTitle: Fuzzy matching and string similarity
lessonTitle: Why exact matching fails and what an edit distance counts
md: A distance counts edits (lower is closer). A similarity is a normalized score (higher is closer). The same raw distance means very different things for short and long strings, so either normalize or make the allowed number of edits depend on length.

courseTitle: Geometric hashing and star-pattern plate solving
lessonTitle: Geometric hashing: basis pairs, a hash table, and votes
md: Geometric hashing moves the expensive work offline: every model is stored under every basis. At query time one correct scene basis is enough, and it never needs to know in advance which model point it corresponds to.

courseTitle: Geospatial indexing and geo filters
lessonTitle: Geohash: interleave the bits, name the cell
md: A shared geohash prefix guarantees closeness: both points are inside the same cell. The reverse is false: two points can be meters apart and share no prefix, because they straddle a cell boundary. Every correct proximity search must look at neighboring cells, not just one prefix.

courseTitle: GPU memory allocators and suballocation
lessonTitle: Why frameworks do not call cudaMalloc for every tensor
md: A caching allocator turns slow, synchronizing driver calls into fast CPU-side bookkeeping. The price is that freed memory is *kept*, so reserved memory, not allocated memory, is what other processes on the GPU see.

courseTitle: GPU memory allocators and suballocation
lessonTitle: Fixed-size suballocation for the KV cache, and diagnosing OOMs
md: All of these allocators are the same pattern at different layers: grab big memory rarely, carve it with your own rules, and choose block sizes that match the workload. Equal sizes kill external fragmentation; growable virtual ranges kill slivers; stream order makes reuse cheap.

courseTitle: GPU memory hierarchy and coalescing
lessonTitle: Case study: one matrix transpose, three kernels
md: These measurements come from older GPUs (Fermi and Kepler in the post, Volta in the guide). Absolute numbers on a current GPU will differ, and larger caches can hide some waste. The sector and bank rules they illustrate are the ones the current CUDA guides still document.

courseTitle: GPU profiling and speed-of-light analysis with Nsight
lessonTitle: The SOL gap: ranking many kernels by what they can return
md: Rank by gap times time share, with an attainable target instead of 100 percent. The biggest gap and the biggest win are usually different kernels, and a gap on a kernel with a small time share is never worth a rewrite.

courseTitle: GraphRAG: entity graphs, communities, and global search
lessonTitle: Why chunk retrieval cannot answer 'what are the main themes?'
md: GraphRAG is not a better retriever for every question. For a specific fact ("Who supplies Rover X2 motors?") plain vector RAG already finds c2, and the paper itself shows vector RAG gives the most *direct* answers. GraphRAG's measured gains are on broad sensemaking questions, the ones that need an understanding of the whole corpus.

courseTitle: GraphRAG: entity graphs, communities, and global search
lessonTitle: Lighter graph RAG: FastGraphRAG, LightRAG, HippoRAG
md: Graph RAG variants differ in where they spend LLM calls: GraphRAG spends heavily at indexing (extraction, summaries, reports) and on map calls per global query; FastGraphRAG cuts extraction; LightRAG drops communities; HippoRAG drops summaries and lets PPR do the multi-hop work.

courseTitle: Transit feeds: GTFS Schedule and GTFS Realtime
lessonTitle: What a GTFS Schedule zip contains and how its tables join
md: A stop can appear twice in one trip, for example on a loop route where the bus starts and ends at the same stop. That is why `stop_sequence`, not `stop_id`, identifies a row of a trip. Code that keys stop times by `stop_id` alone silently overwrites one visit with the other.

courseTitle: Hardware performance counters: measuring why code is slow
lessonTitle: perf record: sampling on overflow, and the skid problem
md: Without precise sampling, the "hot" instruction in `perf annotate` is often the one *after* the slow one, such as the instruction that consumes a load's result. Use `:pp` when you care about individual instructions.

courseTitle: Side channels and hardware security
lessonTitle: Power, EM, sound and faults: physical side channels
md: Physical side channels need the attacker close to the device, but that is exactly the threat model of smart cards, phones, payment terminals, hardware wallets and secure enclaves. Hertzbleed shows the line between physical and remote is not fixed: when power controls frequency, power becomes timing.

courseTitle: Huge pages: 2 MiB and 1 GiB mappings, hugetlbfs and THP
lessonTitle: Transparent Huge Pages: faults, khugepaged and memory bloat
md: `enabled=madvise` turns THP into an opt-in: only regions the application marks with `madvise(MADV_HUGEPAGE)` get huge pages at fault time. The THP doc recommends it where wasted memory matters, and `madvise(MADV_COLLAPSE)` (Linux 6.1+) lets a program request a synchronous collapse of a range.

courseTitle: Hybrid attention and SSM models
lessonTitle: Choosing the ratio and placement, and where hybrids still fall short
md: Design rule of thumb from published ablations: keep roughly 8% to 12% of layers as global attention, spread them evenly, start with an SSM layer, and expect long-context KV savings close to (attention layers in the Transformer you replace) / (attention layers you keep), at equal KV heads: 32 / 4 = 8x for Nemotron-H-8B vs Nemotron-T-8B, not 52 / 4 = 13x.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: What OT and ICS are, and why they are not just IT
md: A common mistake is to treat a plant like an office network: run an aggressive vulnerability scan, push patches overnight, reboot to clean an infection. NIST warns that indiscriminate use of IT practices in OT 'may cause availability and timing disruptions'. In OT the security team works with control engineers, not around them.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: How attacks on physical processes work
md: Three layers stood between the change and an overflow: humans watching the HMI (defeated by the replay), network monitoring (raised an alert at minute 10), and an independent safety system with its own sensor (tripped at minute 26). Design so that the last layer does not share any path with the first two.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: Rules and maps: NERC CIP, IEC 62443, NIST, CISA and ATT&CK for ICS
md: Frameworks tell you what good looks like (62443, NIST), what is mandatory in your sector (NERC CIP for the bulk grid), and how attackers behave (ATT&CK for ICS). Use all three, but remember the cases: most real compromises came through remote access, default passwords and flat networks.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Events, alerts and incidents: when does it become an incident?
md: An incident starts when the attacker acts, not when you declare it. The HSE intrusion began on 18 March 2021 and was declared on 14 May. The gap (dwell time) is what your logs, memory and timeline work must reach back across.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Acquisition: memory, disk images, cloud snapshots and logs
md: Encryption changes the plan. If a disk uses BitLocker or another full-disk encryption, an image taken after power-off is unreadable without the recovery key. Capture what you need from the running system, or make sure the key is in your hands before you shut it down.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Blameless postmortems, lessons learned and tabletop exercises
md: Blameless does not mean nobody is accountable. It means the review asks why the system let a reasonable person make that choice, and fixes the system: alert routing, ownership, tooling, training.

courseTitle: io_uring: asynchronous I/O through shared rings
lessonTitle: Why epoll plus read still costs a syscall per I/O
md: epoll is a **readiness** API: it tells you when an operation *could* succeed, then you do it. io_uring is a **completion** API: you describe the operation (read these bytes into this buffer), and the kernel tells you when it is *done* and what it returned.

courseTitle: jemalloc, mimalloc and tcmalloc internals
lessonTitle: jemalloc: arenas, tcache, bitmap slabs and decay purging
md: Without `background_thread`, purging runs inside your application threads as they call into jemalloc, which adds to their tail latency, and an inactive application delays purging. jemalloc's tuning guide suggests `background_thread:true` where extra jemalloc-managed threads are acceptable.

courseTitle: Jepsen-style fault testing: nemeses, histories and checkers
lessonTitle: Elle: catching isolation anomalies in transactions
md: Elle is sound but not complete: everything it reports is real, but it can miss anomalies. A cycle found is real, yet missing cycles prove nothing: appends never observed by a later read leave gaps in the version order, and predicate anomalies (like phantoms, rows matching a WHERE clause that appear or vanish between two reads in one transaction) are outside its analysis.

courseTitle: Kernel bypass: driving NICs and NVMe from user space (DPDK, SPDK)
lessonTitle: The per-packet budget: why the kernel path runs out of cycles
md: Misconception: bypass is mainly about avoiding copies. The kernel already offers zero-copy paths. At 14.88 Mpps the killers are fixed per-packet costs (interrupts, mode switches, metadata setup, shared locks), which is why minimum-size packets are the benchmark that matters.

courseTitle: Kernel fusion: moving fewer bytes through HBM
lessonTitle: Counting bytes: the chain before and after fusion
md: Fused bytes = what you must read + what you must keep. Everything in between is the saving. For a chain of k unary elementwise ops on the same tensor with no side outputs, eager moves about k times the fused bytes.

courseTitle: Knowledge distillation: teaching a small model with a big one
lessonTitle: When distillation works, when it fails, and what it costs
md: A more accurate teacher is not automatically a better teacher, and a student that improves is not necessarily copying its teacher. Measure student accuracy directly; try a smaller or early-stopped teacher, or a teacher assistant, when the gap is large.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Beyond rounding: pre-RoPE keys, outliers, and FP8 in production
md: Rounding error depends on the range of each group. Pre-RoPE keys, per-channel groups, sparse outliers and an FP16 first token all exist to keep group ranges narrow.

courseTitle: KV cache offloading: tiers, reload vs recompute, and eviction
lessonTitle: Reload or recompute: bytes versus prefill FLOPs
md: Compare bytes over bandwidth with FLOPs over throughput. Fast tiers (host DRAM, RDMA pools) beat prefill at almost any length; slow tiers only pay off for long prompts, big models, or a GPU that is busy anyway.

courseTitle: Clocks: Lamport, vector and hybrid logical clocks
lessonTitle: Lamport clocks: a counter that respects happened-before
md: Lamport clocks do not detect concurrency. From $L(a) < L(b)$ you may conclude only that b did not happen before a. Any code that treats a larger Lamport timestamp as "definitely caused by" is wrong.

courseTitle: Late interaction: ColBERT, PLAID and ColPali
lessonTitle: Searching millions of passages: candidates, centroids, PLAID
md: Cheap approximate scores filter, exact scores decide. PLAID is the same funnel as BM25 followed by a cross-encoder, built inside one model: centroid ids are the cheap representation and decompressed vectors are the precise one.

courseTitle: Latent reasoning: chain of continuous thought (Coconut)
lessonTitle: Latent search: one thought, several frontier nodes
md: BFS-like (breadth-first-search-like) is an interpretation from probing, not a built-in algorithm. Coconut was never trained to search, keeps no explicit visited set, and the parallelism narrows after a couple of thoughts.

courseTitle: Learned indexes: replacing B-tree search with a fitted model
lessonTitle: Error windows, exponential search and monotonic models
md: Always handle the case where the search lands on the edge of the window. With stored min/max bounds, a hit on the boundary is the signal that a non-monotonic model may have pushed the true answer outside.

courseTitle: Learning to rank: from RankNet to LambdaMART
lessonTitle: Why ranking needs its own loss function
md: Ranking metrics depend on the scores only through the **sort**. Learning to rank works around that either by optimizing a smooth stand-in loss (RankNet, ListNet) or, in LambdaRank and LambdaMART, by writing down the gradient we want directly. The coming lessons build each of these.

courseTitle: Linear attention and Gated DeltaNet
lessonTitle: The state is a key-value memory, and it fills up
md: The state is a key-value memory with room for about $d_k$ clean associations per head. Linear attention writes to it with a purely additive rule, so it can neither correct an old association nor make room for new ones.

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: Permission bits: rwx, octal, umask and the kernel's check
md: Owner, then group, then others: the first class that matches is the only one checked. Write octal as 4 for read, 2 for write, 1 for execute, and remember that umask removes bits from every new file.

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: Reading Linux logs: journald, auth.log, failed logins and sudo
md: The journal is stored on disk only if `/var/log/journal` exists or journald is configured with `Storage=persistent`. Otherwise it lives in memory under `/run/log/journal` and is lost at reboot (`journald.conf(5)`). Check this before you need the logs, not after an incident.

courseTitle: LLM-as-judge for relevance labeling
lessonTitle: Circularity, gaming, and running an LLM judge safely
md: Use an LLM judge to label at scale, but never let the measurement and the thing measured share the same model and prompt, and keep a human gold set to check the instrument. When the judge is also a ranking component, its scores stop measuring anything.

courseTitle: Guardrails for LLM applications
lessonTitle: Defense in depth: input, prompt, output and grounding layers
md: Masking the model's input and output does not mask everything else. The AWS docs say Bedrock invocation logs (its record of each model call) keep the original request, and the `match` field of the guardrail trace (the per-request report of what each policy found) contains the original PII value by design. Protect logs and traces separately.

courseTitle: LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management
lessonTitle: Fragmentation, and block tables as page tables
md: Fixed-size blocks plus a per-request table make KV memory behave like virtual memory: allocate on demand, any block fits anywhere, and waste is bounded by one partial block per sequence.

courseTitle: LLM prompting and structured output: from prompts to masked logits
lessonTitle: From regex to JSON Schema: grammars, stacks and real engines
md: The constraint and the prompt are separate channels. A mask can stop the model from writing an illegal token, but it cannot tell the model what the fields mean. If the model never sees the schema (as with llama.cpp's grammar option), describe the fields in the prompt, or the model is forced through a format it does not understand.

courseTitle: LLM query parsing: natural language to structured filters
lessonTitle: Latency budgets, caching and parallel fallback
md: Design for the miss: the parse cache sets the mean, the deadline and keyword fallback set the tail.

courseTitle: Latency and cost tradeoffs for LLM reranking
lessonTitle: Distilled 7B rerankers versus a cross-encoder: choosing a design
md: Do not compare quality numbers across papers as if the setups matched. First-stage retrievers, candidate depth and datasets differ (RankGPT and PRP rerank BM25 top 100; FIRST reranks Contriever top 100). Re-measure on one pipeline.

courseTitle: Local feature matching: Harris, SIFT, ORB and RANSAC
lessonTitle: Why corners make good features: the Harris response
md: Harris scores a window by how much it changes under shifts in every direction. Both eigenvalues of $M$ large means corner; that is what makes a point localizable in two dimensions.

courseTitle: Lock-free stacks and queues: Treiber, Michael-Scott, Vyukov
lessonTitle: Why a preempted lock holder stalls everyone
md: "No mutex in the code" does not make an algorithm lock-free. If one stalled thread can prevent all others from completing, it is blocking, even if it only uses atomic instructions. Michael and Scott call out published queues that are "lock-free but not non-blocking" for exactly this reason, and Vyukov says the same of their own bounded queue (lesson 5).

courseTitle: Lock-free stacks and queues: Treiber, Michael-Scott, Vyukov
lessonTitle: Freeing nodes safely: hazard pointers and epochs
md: Lock-free data structures are two problems: the CAS protocol that keeps the structure consistent, and the reclamation scheme that keeps removed nodes alive until no thread can still be reading them. Get both right, or use a library that has.

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: Why log at all, and why not log everything
md: The log you need is usually older than the moment you learn you need it. Decide what to collect and how long to keep it from the questions an investigation will ask, then pay for that deliberately.

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: Alert quality: precision, recall and the base-rate trap
md: Low precision does not just waste time; it trains people to ignore alerts. Target's alerts were real, but an alert stream that is usually wrong teaches analysts that the next one probably is too. Precision is a security property.

courseTitle: Long context: RoPE scaling, YaRN and Ring Attention
lessonTitle: YaRN: a per-frequency ramp plus attention temperature
md: With dynamic scaling the RoPE of every cached token changes when $s$ changes. The YaRN paper notes the correct implementation caches keys *before* applying RoPE; caching rotated keys silently mixes two different scalings.

courseTitle: Looped and recurrent-depth transformers
lessonTitle: Depth without parameters: what looping a block buys
md: A looped transformer decouples depth from parameter count. $(k \otimes L)$ has $k$ layers of parameters and $kL$ layers of sequential computation.

courseTitle: LoRA, QLoRA and parameter-efficient fine-tuning
lessonTitle: LoRA: a frozen weight plus a trainable low-rank update
md: LoRA does not compress or approximate the pretrained weight. W0 keeps all its information at full rank. Only the *change* learned during fine-tuning is restricted to rank r.

courseTitle: Machine unlearning: removing data and knowledge from trained models
lessonTitle: Unlearning by replacement: Who's Harry Potter and RMU
md: Near-chance accuracy on a multiple-choice proxy shows the model no longer *answers* those questions. It does not show the knowledge is gone from the weights. The WMDP authors say so themselves: because RMU edits only three layers it "perhaps obfuscates knowledge more than unlearns it", and in their appendix fine-tuning on the forget corpus recovered the performance.

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: A safe analysis lab and the analysis workflow
md: Malware can notice it is in a VM and change behaviour (ATT&CK calls this Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion, T1497). An empty or 'boring' run does not prove a file is benign; it may prove only that the sample saw your lab.

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: Command and control: beacons, jitter and Cobalt Strike
md: C2 detection rests on things the operator finds hard to change: timing patterns, the process making the connection, rare destinations, and on-host artifacts. Fortra's own guide shows the traffic shape can be reconfigured (Malleable C2 profiles let an operator change how Beacon's HTTP traffic looks), so content signatures alone age quickly.

courseTitle: Matryoshka embeddings: one vector, many sizes
lessonTitle: How rankings shift as you cut dimensions: Matryoshka vs standard
md: A good Matryoshka prefix gives a coarser version of the full ranking: close items blur together, but far items stay far. A standard model's prefix gives a different, noisy ranking. That is why Matryoshka prefixes are safe for shortlisting.

courseTitle: Megatron-Core performance: TP, PP, SP, CP and MFU
lessonTitle: Distributed optimizer, MoE folding, overlap and measuring MFU
md: Do not compare a paper's achieved TFLOP/s across systems without checking what it counts. Narayanan et al.'s 52% includes recomputation FLOPs; PaLM introduced MFU precisely because HFU depends on implementation choices like rematerialization (another name for recomputation).

courseTitle: Memory fragmentation: why freed memory stays used
lessonTitle: Measuring and fixing fragmentation in production
md: Fix the layer the numbers point at. Slack inside pages (active over allocated) needs objects moved or lifetimes grouped. Unused resident pages (resident over active) need purging or decay. Missing high-order physical blocks need compaction. Reaching for the wrong tool spends CPU and changes nothing.

courseTitle: Memory reclamation: epochs, hazard pointers, RCU
lessonTitle: Why freeing a removed node is the hard part
md: Removing a node and freeing it are different events. Every scheme in this course defers the free until no thread can still hold a reference taken before the removal.

courseTitle: Memory safety bugs: overflows, use-after-free and friends
lessonTitle: What memory safety means and why breaking it is dangerous
md: C and C++ do not check bounds or lifetimes for you. Every array index, every length and every `free` is a promise the programmer must keep by hand. Memory safety bugs are what happens when one promise is broken, and the attacker gets to choose the input.

courseTitle: Memory safety bugs: overflows, use-after-free and friends
lessonTitle: Uninitialized memory and type confusion
md: Uninitialized reads leak what came before; type confusion reinterprets what is there. Both are fixed the same way in spirit: never let code read bytes whose meaning it has not established, by initializing first and checking tags before use.

courseTitle: Metric learning and re-identification
lessonTitle: Batch hard: mining the hardest pairs inside a P x K batch
md: Sample P identities x K images so every batch contains positives and look-alike negatives, then mine within the batch. Mining becomes a max and a min over a distance matrix you already have.

courseTitle: Microbenchmarking pitfalls: when the number lies
lessonTitle: Measurement bias: layout, link order and JIT profiles
md: Misconception: "disabling ASLR and pinning the CPU makes my benchmark correct". They reduce run-to-run noise, which narrows intervals. A narrow interval around a biased setup is a confidently wrong answer.

courseTitle: Miles: production RL post-training forked from slime
lessonTitle: Moving a trillion parameters, and surviving dead engines
md: The Miles fault-tolerance page is marked **outdated**: it describes the pre-refactor stack, and new machinery is still being merged. Also note that P2P writes are bounded by `--p2p-transfer-timeout` (default 30 s) and a failed write fails the update; the docs state there is no automatic retry or fallback to broadcast.

courseTitle: ML for systems: learned indexes, caching and scheduling
lessonTitle: Deploying learned policies: inference budgets, drift and guardrails
md: Reported speedups are relative to specific baselines on specific traces: B-LRU on six CDN traces, a tuned weighted fair scheduler on TPC-H mixes, a read-optimized B-tree on read-only integer keys. A different workload, or a stronger baseline, can shrink the gain to zero.

courseTitle: Serving many LoRA adapters on one base model
lessonTitle: Merge, swap, or compute the adapter on the fly
md: Unmerged does not mean easy. Requests in one batch use adapters with different ranks and different sequence lengths, so padding everything into one batched matmul wastes work. S-LoRA's variant that copies adapters into contiguous memory and uses padded batched matmul (S-LoRA-bmm) was much slower than the version with custom kernels, GPU functions written for exactly this mixed-rank job.

courseTitle: Multi-query retrieval: many phrasings, one fused result
lessonTitle: Union versus RRF, and deduplicating by document id
md: RRF rewards agreement between phrasings. A relevant document that only one phrasing finds stays low, and a junk document that two phrasings share can outrank it. That is why the quality of the phrasings matters as much as their number.

courseTitle: Multi-token prediction: training GPTs to look ahead
lessonTitle: From one target per position to n targets per position
md: Common misconception: an MTP model does not have to emit several tokens per step. Gloeckle et al. use only the next-token head for ordinary decoding. The other heads are optional, and lesson 5 shows how they can be reused to draft tokens for faster decoding.

courseTitle: Muon, Shampoo and SOAP: optimizers that treat weights as matrices
lessonTitle: Shampoo: one preconditioner for the rows, one for the columns
md: A frequent mistake is to read $L^{-1/4}$ as an elementwise power. It is a *matrix* power: eigendecompose $L = Q \Lambda Q^\top$ and take $Q \Lambda^{-1/4} Q^\top$. That needs float32 (or better) and an eigensolver, which is why roots are only refreshed every $f$ steps.

courseTitle: muP: tune a small model, transfer hyperparameters to a large one
lessonTitle: What breaks in SP after a single training step
md: Common misconception: "SP is broken only because the learning rate is too large for big models." Lowering it uniformly fixes the exploding layers but freezes others, such as the input embeddings. The issue is the *relative* scaling between layers.

courseTitle: Mutexes, spinlocks and futexes: how locks really wait
lessonTitle: The futex: sleep on an address, wake by address
md: FUTEX_WAIT says "sleep only if the word still holds the value I based my decision on". That expected-value check, done atomically by the kernel, is what makes lost wake-ups impossible.

courseTitle: MVCC and transaction isolation levels
lessonTitle: Read Committed vs Repeatable Read: when the snapshot is taken
md: Read Committed is not a weaker form of a single consistent view. Each statement sees one snapshot, but an updating statement can also see newer versions of the rows it is about to change, so a single UPDATE or DELETE can mix two moments in time. The docs call it unsuitable for commands with complex search conditions.

courseTitle: Named entity recognition: tagging spans in text
lessonTitle: BIO, IOB1 and BIOES: tag sets that make spans decodable
md: The repair rule is not cosmetic: it changes your score. [seqeval](https://github.com/chakki-works/seqeval) documents that for gold `B-NP I-NP O` and prediction `I-NP I-NP O`, its default mode (which mimics the conlleval Perl script) gives precision, recall and F1 of 1.00, while `mode='strict'` with `scheme=IOB2` gives 0.00. Same predictions, two different papers' worth of difference. Always say which mode you used.

courseTitle: Native sparse attention: NSA and DeepSeek Sparse Attention
lessonTitle: DeepSeek Sparse Attention: a lightning indexer picks tokens
md: Neither NSA nor DSA shrinks the KV cache. NSA adds compressed and per-branch keys; DSA adds an indexer key per token. Both cut the bytes *read and computed* per query. Also, DSA's indexer is still $O(L^2)$ over a sequence, just with a much smaller constant.

courseTitle: NeMo RL: NVIDIA's Ray-based post-training library
lessonTitle: One controller, many RL Actors: the NeMo RL architecture
md: The single controller does not mean all tensors flow through one process. Large transfers, especially weight refit, go over channels the controller sets up (CUDA IPC or NCCL), not through the controller itself. A CUDA IPC (inter-process communication) handle is a small token that lets another process on the same machine open the same GPU memory without copying it.

courseTitle: Network attacks and defences
lessonTitle: BGP hijacks and route leaks: the MyEtherWallet case
md: A BGP hijack does not need to touch your servers or your users' networks. It moves traffic somewhere else on the internet, where your TLS certificate, DNSSEC signatures and user training are the remaining defences.

courseTitle: How networks work, seen by an attacker and a defender
lessonTitle: From bits on a wire to packets
md: Every packet is a header plus a payload. Every device on the path must read the header to deliver it, and can read the payload too unless it is encrypted. Both facts drive almost everything in network security.

courseTitle: How networks work, seen by an attacker and a defender
lessonTitle: HTTPS and TLS at a glance: what encryption hides and what it does not
md: TLS protects the content of one connection between two endpoints. It does not hide who talks to whom, it does not make the server trustworthy, and it does not protect data once it is decrypted at either end.

courseTitle: NUMA: placing memory and threads on multi-socket machines
lessonTitle: Memory policies: local, bind, preferred and interleave
md: Policy = mode + nodes + scope, applied at allocation time. Use bind for strict isolation, preferred when spilling over is acceptable, interleave for big shared data, and leave private per-thread data on the default local policy.

courseTitle: Object detection and counting
lessonTitle: What a detector outputs, and how two boxes are compared
md: A detector outputs a variable-size set of (box, class, score) triples, and IoU between boxes is the measure every later stage builds on.

courseTitle: Object detection and counting
lessonTitle: Counting objects: by detection, by density, by tracking
md: Pick the counting method by scene: detection when objects are separable and you need locations, density maps for dense crowds where boxes fail, and tracking plus line or region events for video, where the same object appears in many frames.

courseTitle: Observability: metrics, traces, dashboards and SLOs
lessonTitle: Counters, gauges, histograms, and the quantile you must not average
md: Never compute a rate as last value minus first value over a counter. One restart in the window turns a positive rate into a large negative number, and `rate()` exists precisely to handle that case for you.

courseTitle: OCR and document understanding: from pixels to fields
lessonTitle: Why OCR is a pipeline: find the text, then read it
md: OCR is a chain: detect, then recognize, then order and extract. Each stage only sees the previous stage's output, so an early error silently becomes a wrong field later.

courseTitle: OS security, privilege and isolation
lessonTitle: The kernel/user boundary: rings and the system call door
md: User programs run in ring 3 and can only ask; the kernel runs in ring 0 and decides. A system call is the only door between them. Sandboxing is mostly the art of closing doors and narrowing what each open door accepts.

courseTitle: OS security, privilege and isolation
lessonTitle: Sandboxes: Chrome's broker model, macOS and iOS
md: A broker is only as good as its request checking. A broker that performs "open this path" for any path a renderer names has turned itself into a tool for the attacker. That failure has a name, the confused deputy, and it is the subject of lesson 15.

courseTitle: Building large projects from source (CMake, CUDA builds)
lessonTitle: Targets, PUBLIC vs PRIVATE, and why links fail
md: Declare every real dependency on the target that uses it, with the narrowest correct scope: PRIVATE if only the .cpp files use it, PUBLIC if your headers expose it, INTERFACE if only your headers do. CMake then derives include paths, definitions and link order for you.

courseTitle: CI pipelines and test suites: from red checks to reliable tests
lessonTitle: Diagnosing and fixing flaky tests: order, state and timing
md: Do not add `@pytest.mark.flaky` or `xfail` to a test your PR broke. Maintainers read that as hiding a failure. If you believe a failure is pre-existing flakiness, show evidence: the same test failing on `main` or on other PRs, or a seed that reproduces it without your change.

courseTitle: Code review: responding to and giving review
lessonTitle: Review by email: patch versions and trailer tags
md: You may not add a Reviewed-by, Tested-by or Acked-by tag for someone just because they said nice things. The kernel guide says these need the named person's explicit permission; only Cc:, Reported-by: and Suggested-by: can be added with implicit permission.

courseTitle: Contribution norms: CONTRIBUTING, issues, conduct and AI policies
lessonTitle: AI-assisted contributions: label it, keep a human in the loop, or not
md: Before using an AI tool on a contribution, find the project's policy (CONTRIBUTING, developer docs, or the docs on patch submission). Then: never submit what you cannot explain, disclose as the project asks, and never let a tool add your sign-off.

courseTitle: Git workflow for pull requests: fork, branch, rebase, sign-off
lessonTitle: Pushing rewritten history: --force-with-lease and its limits
md: `--force-with-lease` says "overwrite only if the remote is still what I last fetched". Add `--force-if-includes` so a fetch alone does not count as having seen the remote's commits.

courseTitle: Open source licenses, CLAs and the DCO
lessonTitle: Inbound licensing: inbound=outbound and contributor agreements
md: The most common CLA failure is an email mismatch: the commits use a personal or unregistered address while the agreement (or the employer's group) lists another. Fix the author email and rewrite the commits, not the agreement.

courseTitle: Performance PRs: benchmark evidence and regression checks
lessonTitle: Is the difference real? t-tests, U tests and p-values
md: Significant is not the same as large. benchstat's docs stress that with enough low-noise data even very small changes become significant. Report the size of the change and its spread, and use the test only to answer "is this more than noise?"

courseTitle: Reproducing bugs: minimal repros, delta debugging and git bisect
lessonTitle: What a maintainer needs: a failure they can run themselves
md: A bug report's first job is to let the maintainer make the failure happen themselves. Everything else in the report (description, guesses about the cause) comes second.

courseTitle: Reproducing bugs: minimal repros, delta debugging and git bisect
lessonTitle: Intermittent bugs, seeds, and environment differences
md: A flaky repro is not done until it fails every time or you know its failure rate. Pin seeds and inputs, report versions, and repeat runs enough times that a PASS means something.

courseTitle: Writing a reviewable pull request
lessonTitle: Self-review the diff, then use drafts to signal readiness
md: Self-review first, then mark ready. A reviewable PR is focused, explained, clean, and honestly labeled as draft or ready.

courseTitle: PagedAttention and prefix caching
lessonTitle: RadixAttention, cache-aware scheduling, and when caching pays
md: Prefix caching never changes outputs. It reuses KV for exactly the same tokens instead of recomputing it, so its effects are on speed and memory (outputs can differ only by the tiny floating-point noise any change in batching causes). It helps exactly as much as prefill dominates the work and prefixes repeat.

courseTitle: Penetration testing methodology and recon
lessonTitle: Verifying findings safely, without becoming the incident
md: Verify with the least risky evidence that answers the question. Write down the confidence and what you chose not to do. Stop immediately when you see signs that someone else got there first.

courseTitle: perf and flame graphs
lessonTitle: Broken stacks: frame pointers, DWARF, LBR and symbols
md: Missing callers, a detached tower over [unknown], or hex instead of names are not hot spots. They are profiler blind spots. Fix frame pointers or symbols before you trust the picture.

courseTitle: Phishing, social engineering and email security
lessonTitle: Why people are the most attacked surface
md: The one thing to remember: phishing attacks a decision, not a machine. Defences therefore come in three kinds: stop the message arriving, make the action harmless if taken (for example passkeys), and make the final step need a second check (for example calling the supplier on a known number).

courseTitle: Phishing, social engineering and email security
lessonTitle: Lookalike domains and homoglyphs
md: Misconception: "hover over the link and check the domain" solves this. A homoglyph domain can look correct even when you hover, and on phones you often cannot hover. Machine checks (skeletons, domain age) and phishing-resistant logins (lesson 12) carry the load; human checks are a backup.

courseTitle: Pose estimation: heatmaps, grouping, OKS and joint angles
lessonTitle: Heatmaps: training targets, argmax and sub-pixel decoding
md: The network never outputs coordinates. It outputs heatmaps, and a small hand-written decoder (argmax, quarter-cell shift, scale by stride, undo the crop) turns them into numbers. Bugs in that decoder, such as swapping x and y or forgetting the crop offset, look like a bad model.

courseTitle: Pre-filtering vs post-filtering with metadata
lessonTitle: Filtering inside the graph walk, and when the graph falls apart
md: Filtering during traversal is the right default for medium selectivity, but it has two failure modes at low $s$: a strict walk gets cut off (disconnection), and a walk-through degenerates into visiting about $k/s$ nodes. Both point to the same escape hatch: when matches are few, scan them directly.

courseTitle: Privilege escalation and lateral movement
lessonTitle: Linux escalation 1: reading sudo rules like an auditor
md: Misconception: "NOPASSWD is the dangerous part." It does remove a hurdle for an intruder who has a shell but not the password (a web shell, a stolen SSH key). But a rule that leads to a shell is a root grant with or without a password prompt. Fix what the command can do first, then decide on the password.

courseTitle: Process reward models: grading reasoning one step at a time
lessonTitle: How a PRM is trained and how it scores a solution
md: A PRM is a per-step classifier read off in one forward pass. Training labels stop at the first error. To compare solutions you reduce step scores to one number; product and minimum perform similarly, but product quietly favours shorter solutions.

courseTitle: Processes, threads and the real cost of a context switch
lessonTitle: Counting switches and designing around them
md: Misconception: "more threads means more parallelism." Parallelism is capped by the number of cores. Past that, extra CPU-bound threads only take turns: they add involuntary switches, push answers later, and make threads evict each other's cache. Extra threads help only when they spend time blocked, as in the I/O scene.

courseTitle: Automatic prompt optimization: APE, OPRO and DSPy
lessonTitle: DSPy: signatures, modules and optimizers
md: Every bootstrap and search optimizer trusts the metric. The DSPy docs warn that a non-deterministic metric (for example an LLM judge) makes the chosen demos "a function of metric noise as much as program quality". Make the metric deterministic where you can, validate any LLM judge against humans first, and keep a held-out set.

courseTitle: Python for security work: parsing, automating and calling APIs
lessonTitle: Why security teams script, and your first Python program
md: A script is the steps you would do by hand, written down once so they run the same way on every line. Its biggest risk is not crashing; it is quietly counting the wrong thing.

courseTitle: Python for security work: parsing, automating and calling APIs
lessonTitle: Hashing files and checking them against known-bad lists
md: A hash match is strong evidence; a hash miss proves nothing. Security researcher David Bianco's [Pyramid of Pain](https://detect-respond.blogspot.com/2013/03/the-pyramid-of-pain.html) puts hash values at the bottom because changing a single byte gives the attacker a brand new hash. Use hash lists to catch known copies quickly, never as the only control.

courseTitle: Query expansion: synonyms, feedback and LLM rewrites
lessonTitle: Synonym expansion on the toy corpus: recall up, precision at risk
md: Misconception: expansion always helps. It helps when the added words mean the same thing **in this query's context**. *auto* means automobile in d6 but automatic in d9; a list that ignores sense trades recall for false matches. Here the bad synonym cost nothing at the top only because the good documents happened to score higher.

courseTitle: RaBitQ and binary quantization: 1-bit vectors with error bounds
lessonTitle: Plain binary quantization: one sign bit per dimension
md: Sign bits only carry information if coordinates are spread around zero. Qdrant's docs say binary quantization needs a *centered distribution* of vector components. If every coordinate is positive, every bit is 1 and all vectors look identical; non-negative data such as SIFT (scale-invariant feature transform) image descriptors comes close to this. Lesson 2 measures this failure.

courseTitle: Raft and Paxos consensus
lessonTitle: Raft leader election: terms, votes and randomized timeouts
md: `currentTerm`, `votedFor` (the candidate this server voted for in the current term) and the log must reach stable storage *before* a server answers an RPC. If a server voted, crashed, and forgot its vote, it could vote again in the same term for a different candidate, and two leaders could be elected for one term.

courseTitle: Retrieval-augmented generation: the pipeline and its failures
lessonTitle: Evaluating retrieval and generation separately
md: Read the metrics as a grid. Low context recall: a **retrieval** problem. High context recall but low faithfulness: a **generation** problem. High faithfulness but wrong answer: the context itself was wrong or stale, an **index** problem.

courseTitle: Ranking metrics: precision@k, recall@k, NDCG, MRR
lessonTitle: nDCG precisely: gain, discount, log base and the ideal
md: nDCG has four knobs: the gain (linear or exponential), the discount (modern log2(i+1) or the original base b form), the cutoff k, and where the ideal comes from (all qrels, not the run). Report all four or your number cannot be reproduced.

courseTitle: RDMA: kernel-bypass networking with verbs
lessonTitle: InfiniBand, RoCEv2 and iWARP: what carries the packets
md: RoCEv2 gets RDMA onto ordinary routed Ethernet only by making that Ethernet (nearly) lossless with PFC, then taming PFC's side effects with end-to-end congestion control such as DCQCN. Loss is still possible from corruption or misconfiguration, and go-back-N recovery makes it expensive.

courseTitle: Real-time multiplayer networking: WebSockets and state sync
lessonTitle: Showing other players: interpolation and lag compensation
md: The local player lives in the **present** (prediction); everyone else is shown in the **past** (interpolation); the server reconciles the two when it matters (lag compensation).

courseTitle: Recommender systems and cold start
lessonTitle: Cold start: content for new items, bandits for new users
md: Cold start is a data problem, so the fixes are other data: content features for new items, context and popularity for new users, then controlled exploration to collect the interactions CF needs.

courseTitle: Relational operators: joins, aggregation and planning
lessonTitle: When each join wins: row counts, probes and memory
md: `work_mem` is a limit per sort or hash operation, not per query. A plan with three hash joins and a sort can use several multiples of it, and many sessions can do so at once. Raising it globally to fix one query can exhaust memory.

courseTitle: Replication and quorums: N, R, W and what they really buy you
lessonTitle: Failures: sloppy quorums, hinted handoff and repair
md: A write that *fails* (fewer than W acks before the timeout) is not rolled back. It may sit on a minority of replicas and later spread through repair or hints. The Cassandra docs warn that without blocking read repair such a write "may be visible in one read, and then disappear in a subsequent read". "Failed" means "outcome unknown", not "did not happen".

courseTitle: Reward hacking: when optimizing the score breaks the task
lessonTitle: Catching hacks: CoT monitors, obfuscation, generalization
md: Use the CoT monitor to **detect** problems and fix environments, but avoid strong optimization pressure directly on the CoT. Baker et al. call the cost of keeping CoTs monitorable (for example a slightly less capable or more expensive model) a **monitorability tax**. They also note that even patching only the bugs a monitor finds may put slight pressure toward hacks it cannot see.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Treating risk: accept, mitigate, transfer, avoid
md: "Transfer" moves money, not responsibility. An insurer may pay for forensics and claims, and a contract may make a vendor liable, but regulators and customers still hold you accountable for the breach of your data, and insurers can deny claims when the controls you declared on the application form were not really in place (lesson 17).

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: SOC 2: trust services criteria, Type I vs II, and your evidence
md: SOC 2 is a CPA's opinion on your controls against the Trust Services Criteria. Type I: designed and in place on a date. Type II: operating effectively over a period, tested by sampling. Most of the evidence is ordinary engineering records, if your process creates them.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Third-party risk: questionnaires, SBOMs and concentration risk
md: Tier vendors by access and criticality; use standard questionnaires and independent reports with their scope, exceptions and user-entity controls; write breach notice and exit into contracts; collect SBOMs so a new CVE becomes a query; and record shared dependencies as their own concentration risks with fallbacks.

courseTitle: RL post-training infrastructure at scale
lessonTitle: The long tail: why one response can idle a whole cluster
md: Partial rollouts are not free. A trajectory stitched from segments generated by several policy versions is off-policy data. Kimi notes some segments can be excluded from the loss; AReaL's interruptible rollouts face the same issue and handle it with a modified PPO objective.

courseTitle: Roofline model and GPU bandwidth measurement
lessonTitle: Placing GEMM, softmax and LLM decode on the roofline
md: Intensity is not fixed for a given operation. It depends on shape (thin GEMMs fall left), precision (FP8 halves the bytes per element and so doubles intensity), and how well the implementation reuses data. A naive GEMM that rereads inputs from DRAM can be memory bound even at 8192 cubed.

courseTitle: Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)
lessonTitle: Why fuse ranks instead of scores
md: An RRF score is not a relevance probability. Its size depends on k and on how many lists were fused (Azure AI Search notes each query contributes at most about $1/k$), so do not apply a fixed threshold to it across queries or configurations.

courseTitle: Rust in the Linux kernel: safe abstractions over unsafe C
lessonTitle: Bindings, helpers, abstractions: the layers under a Rust driver
md: Misconception: "Rust drivers do not need cleanup code." They need exactly as much cleanup as C drivers. The difference is that it lives once in a `Drop` impl (yours or an abstraction's) and runs on every path automatically, including early returns from `?`.

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: The scheduling cycle: select_cpu, enqueue, dispatch, run
md: Where a task finally runs is decided when it lands in a local DSQ, usually inside `ops.dispatch()` on the CPU that is asking for work. `select_cpu` is an optimization: matching the final CPU saves a bit of work, and picking an idle CPU wakes it up.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: Threat, vulnerability, exploit, payload and risk
md: A vulnerability is not a risk by itself. A severe bug in software you do not run, or on a machine with no network connection, may carry very little risk. A boring weakness on an internet-facing system that attackers already scan for can carry a lot. Lesson 6 turns this into a patching order.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: EternalBlue and WannaCry: a patch, a leak and a worm
